info.description: Everything Argus does, it does through this API — the browser is one client of it, not a privileged one. That is the whole extension story: a script, a cron job, an agent hook or another machine can do anything the app can, with no plugin to install and nothing running inside the page. **Every route is behind the same token**, in an `Authorization: Bearer …` header or a `?token=` query for the places a header cannot go — a WebSocket, an ``, a page opened directly. Anyone holding it can run anything you can: treat it like an SSH key. **Everything lives under `/api`.** Nothing outside it answers with data, this document included, so a single rule guards the lot. The most useful thing to build against first is `POST /api/bell` — that is how an agent tells you it has finished or wants you, and it needs nothing but curl.
info.summary: Watch your agents run in tmux, and read what they produced.

post.description: Called by an agent hook, or by anything else that knows it has finished.
post.summary: Ring: something finished, or wants you

get.description: Which agents on this machine are set up to ring, and which are not.

schema.title: Response Wired Api Bell Wiring Get

get.summary: Which agents on this machine are set up to ring

post.description:
Do the setting up, or take it back out.

This writes into the agents' own configuration files, which is exactly the work the
person would otherwise be doing by hand — and it is additive: an event they have
already claimed is reported, never overwritten, and a copy of each file as it was
before Argus first touched it is kept beside it.

schema.title: Response Rewire Api Bell Wiring Post

post.summary: Set the agents up to ring, or undo it

get.description:
Everything rung after `since`.

The answer always carries the current sequence, so a browser that has just started —
or one that was away long enough for the list to roll over — can mark where "now" is
and catch up from there rather than replaying a morning's worth of notifications.

Deciding *that* is the browser's job, not this one's. An earlier version tried to help
by treating `since=0` as "you have just arrived, here is nothing", and it meant a
server that had not rung yet handed out `seq: 0`, took `since=0` back for ever after,
and stayed silent for the life of the page.
get.summary: What has rung since a given point

get.description:
Bells as they happen, over one connection that stays open.

This is what makes a background tab work. It also needs no HTTPS, unlike the
browser's own notifications — the sound and the tab title are what is left over
plain http, and both want to happen the moment it rings rather than a minute later.
get.summary: Bells as they happen, over one open connection

schema.title: Response Server Info Api Config Get

get.summary: What this server allows

get.description:
Names, when each was added and when each was last used. Never the tokens: only a
hash of those is kept, and the plain form existed once, when it was created.

schema.title: Response List Devices Api Devices Get

get.summary: The devices that may get in

post.description:
Mints one and returns it **once**. There is no way to see it again — the file holds
only a hash — which is the same bargain GitHub makes for a personal access token, and
for the same reason.

Only the token in the config may do this. A device cannot mint another, so a phone
that is lost cannot be used to grow its own foothold.

schema.title: Response Add Device Api Devices Post

post.summary: Give a device its own token

delete.description:
Takes effect on the next request that device makes: the file is re-read every time
a token is presented, precisely so that revoking is not something you have to restart
for.

schema.title: Response Drop Device Api Devices  Device Id  Delete

post.description:
The token is untouched: this is the label, not the key. Renaming does not sign
anything out, which is the whole reason it is a separate action from revoking.

schema.title: Response Rename Device Api Devices  Device Id  Post

get.summary: Download a file under its own name

schema.title: Response List Favourites Api Favourites Get

get.summary: Pinned folders, kept on the server

schema.title: Response Toggle Favourite Api Favourites Post

get.summary: Read a file, or its tail if it is large

schema.title: Response List Dir Api Files Get

get.summary: List a folder

schema.title: Response Copy Api Fs Copy Post
Response Delete Api Fs Delete Post

post.description: Which of these words are files? Read-only, and jailed like everything else.

schema.title: Response Locate Api Fs Locate Post
Response Mkdir Api Fs Mkdir Post
Response Move Api Fs Move Post
Response Rename Api Fs Rename Post

post.description:
Receive files into a directory.

Each one is streamed to a dotted part-file and renamed into place only once it is
complete, so an interrupted upload never leaves a truncated file wearing the real
name — which for a 40 GB fastq is the difference between "retry" and "silent
corruption three steps down the pipeline".

schema.title: Response Upload Api Fs Upload Post

get.description:
What a folder actually weighs, added up by hand.

Apparent size, the sum of the file sizes — the number that matches what you see in a
listing, rather than the blocks on disk, which sparse files and compression make a
different question.

schema.title: Response Usage Api Fs Usage Get

get.summary: What a folder weighs, walked on request

post.description:
Save an edited text file.

Two things must hold. The file cannot have moved on since it was read — otherwise a
phone would quietly undo whatever the running job just wrote — and a file too large
to have been previewed whole must never be saved from a preview, because that
preview was only its tail.

schema.title: Response Write Api Fs Write Post
Response Drop Worktree Api Git Worktree Delete

post.description:
A second checkout of the same repository, on its own branch.

Writing, so it needs `--allow-write`: it makes a directory, and one that git will go
on believing in until somebody removes it properly.

schema.title: Response Add Worktree Api Git Worktree Post

post.summary: Add a working directory on its own branch

schema.title: Response List Worktrees Api Git Worktrees Get

get.summary: The working directories of a repository

delete.description:
Everything, or everything before a cutoff given in seconds.

The deletion is recorded like any other change — the middleware sees this request and
writes it down — so the journal always says that it was emptied, when, and from where.

schema.title: Response Clear Journal Api Journal Delete

delete.summary: Empty the journal, or the old part of it

get.description:
Most recent first. Only the token from the config may read it: a record that a
possibly-stolen device can read is a record that tells whoever took it what you can see.

schema.title: Response Read Journal Api Journal Get

get.summary: What has been done here, and what was refused

post.description:
Anyone can translate the catalogue and add it here; it is a flat JSON object
keyed by the English strings, so it needs no tooling to produce.

schema.title: Response Import Language Api Language Post

post.summary: Add or replace a language catalogue

schema.title: Response One Language Api Language  Code  Get

get.summary: One language catalogue

schema.title: Response List Languages Api Languages Get

get.summary: The interface languages available

get.description:
The list a browser is allowed to pick from, and whether each one is really here.

`available` is `null` when the answer is not knowable: a command with a pipe or a
`&&` in it is a shell line rather than a program, and checking the PATH for it would
be a guess dressed as a fact.
get.summary: What this machine can start

get.description:
Everything a board watching several machines needs, and nothing it does not.

This is the one door a watcher token opens, and the same answer a machine
announces to a board that cannot reach it.
get.summary: What is happening on this machine, in one cheap call

get.description:
Find a string in a PDF and say which pages it is on.

The browser's own viewer has a search box on a desktop and nothing at all on a phone,
and inside an iframe Ctrl+F searches the page around it rather than the document. So
the text is extracted here and the viewer is sent to the page.

schema.title: Response Pdf Search Api Pdf Search Get

get.summary: Find text in a PDF, page by page

schema.title: Response List Ports Api Ports Get

get.summary: What is listening, and what is holding it

post.description:
Opening a port also hands back the cookie the proxied page needs: its own
stylesheets and scripts cannot carry an Authorization header.
post.summary: Open or close a port for proxying

get.description:
The names, and whether each is up right now. Not the commands.

A board needs to know what it may ask for and what is already happening; it has no
use for the shell line, and every extra thing on the wire is one more thing a leaked
board leaks.
get.summary: What this machine offers to start and stop

post.description:
`action` is start or stop, and `name` must be something this machine published.

No command arrives in this request and none ever will. That is what keeps a watcher
token nearly worthless: the worst anything holding it can do is start or stop what is
written in this machine's own config.

schema.title: Response Run One Api Runnable  Name   Action  Post

post.summary: Start or stop one of them

get.summary: Find files by name under a folder

post.description:
Stops the server. Nothing here can start it again.

That asymmetry is the whole character of this endpoint: every tmux session carries on
untouched — Argus is a client, not their parent — but the only way back to this page
is a shell on this machine, or a supervisor that restarts it. Which is why it takes
`may_stop_argus` on top of `may_run`, and why the answer says so.

get.description:
Just enough to notice a file has changed: a window watching a report being
regenerated polls this rather than re-downloading the whole thing.

schema.title: Response Stat Path Api Stat Get

get.summary: Size and modification time, for watching a file
CPU, memory, swap, GPUs, disks, uptime

get.description: The last thing copied inside tmux, so it can reach the device's clipboard.

schema.title: Response Tmux Buffer Api Tmux Buffer Get

get.summary: The last thing copied inside tmux

get.description: Is this session showing history rather than the live end?

schema.title: Response Read Copy Mode Api Tmux Copymode Get

get.summary: Is this session showing history rather than the live end

post.description: Leave history and return to the live end.

schema.title: Response Exit Copy Mode Api Tmux Copymode Post

get.description:
Where this session actually is, and how well that is known.

Not the same thing as the folder a desk was given: that one decides where a file
browser lands and what a hand-over sentence says, while this is the directory the
work is really happening in. Telling the other agent to look somewhere its
counterpart never was is a whole round wasted.

`cwd_source` says where the answer came from, best first — `agent` (the program said
so, in the pane option `@argus_cwd`), `process` (read from the process that holds the
terminal), `tmux` (tmux's own observation), `start` (the directory the pane was made
in). `cwd_live` is false only for the last, which is history rather than news.

schema.title: Response Pane Directory Api Tmux Cwd Get

get.summary: The directory a session is really in

post.description: Killing a session ends everything running in it. The UI asks first.

schema.title: Response Kill Session Api Tmux Kill Post

post.description:
Create a session, start a launcher in it, wait for it to settle, type the prompt.

Only a launcher **named in the config** can be started, which is what keeps this from
being "run anything" — the terminal next to it always was, but an endpoint that takes
a command line is a different thing to leave on a network.

The return says what actually happened rather than only that it worked: whether the
thing settled before the wait ran out, and whether the return was pressed. A prompt
typed into an agent that was still drawing its banner is the failure this is designed
around, so when `ready` is false the text is left sitting there unsent, for you.

schema.title: Response Launch Agent Api Tmux Launch Post

post.summary: Start an agent, with its first instruction

schema.title: Response New Session Api Tmux New Post
Response Rename Session Api Tmux Rename Post
Response Sessions Api Tmux Sessions Get

get.summary: Every tmux session on this server

post.description:
Make every session pick up the configuration file.

tmux options are per-server, so one source-file reaches every session on it —
there is nothing to do per session. The file is tried on a throwaway server first,
because sourcing runs it and a bad line can end the server everything is in.

schema.title: Response Source Conf Api Tmux Source Post

post.summary: Hand the tmux config to every session, after trying it safely

post.description:
Put a look on one session, live.

A look in the config file belongs to the server and dresses everything; this
dresses the session named and leaves the rest alone. Only style options are
accepted, from a fixed list — see tmux.STYLE_OPTIONS.

schema.title: Response Dress Api Tmux Style Post

post.summary: Dress one session, without touching the config

get.description:
Answers immediately from a day-old cache; the question is only asked of GitHub
when that cache is stale. Switched off, it answers about this machine and stops
there, which is also what it does when there is no way out to the network.
get.summary: What is running here, and whether anything newer exists

get.description:
Which agents here can tell Argus the folder they consider current.

Only Claude Code can: it hands its status line hook `workspace.current_dir`. Nothing
outside an agent can work that out — an agent never moves its own process — so this is
the difference between a mark that follows the work and one that names where the
session started.

schema.title: Response Where Wired Api Where Wiring Get

get.summary: Which agents are set up to say which folder they are in

post.description:
Do the setting up, or take it back out.

The same bargain as the bell: it writes into the agent's own configuration, keeps a copy
of the file as it was before Argus first touched it, reports a status line you wrote
yourself rather than replacing it, and removes only what carries our own marker.

schema.title: Response Where Rewire Api Where Wiring Post

post.summary: Set the agents up to say where they are, or undo it
